title: Algebraic branching programs versus formulas
formal: For a fixed field F, is \(VF_{F} a\) proper subclass of \(VBP_{F}\)? Equivalently, is there a family \((f_{n})\) of polynomials of polynomially bounded degree in polynomially many commuting variables that has polynomial-size algebraic branching programs over F but no polynomial-size algebraic formulas over F? The field is a parameter of the question, as in the source; a result must state the fields to which it applies.
context:
A formula is a tree: an intermediate result used in two places must be copied. A branching program can share subpaths, and its output combines the products along all paths.

Every polynomial-size algebraic formula has a polynomial-size branching program. The question is whether this containment hides a strict difference in expressive power.

The source discusses a branching-program family that already requires more than a particular small depth in polynomial-size formulas. That does not rule out polynomial-size formulas of unrestricted depth.

The January 2026 paper recalls a known separation between syntactically multilinear formulas and branching programs. An unrestricted formula computing a multilinear output need not itself be syntactically multilinear, so that theorem does not settle VF versus VBP.
why: Separates two fundamental models of algebraic computation and asks whether sharing path computations gives a polynomial-versus-superpolynomial advantage over arithmetic trees.
status_note: Recovered the exact containment from the source and checked subsequent work through 12 September 2026, including the January 2026 multilinear paper. No unrestricted resolution was located. The May revision notice for ECCC TR26-043 reports a gap in that separate barrier claim, which is not used as an established result here.

progress.text: The source explicitly records \(VF \subseteq\) VBP as a containment whose strictness is unknown and distinguishes it from depth-restricted lower bounds.
The later paper studies the restricted multilinear hierarchy and recounts its known formula-versus-branching-program separation; it does not claim the general separation.

definitions: A polynomial family has \(f_{n}\in F[x_{1},\ldots ,x_{m(n)}]\), where \(m(n)\) and the total degree of \(f_{n}\) are at most \(n^{a}+a\) for some fixed a. An algebraic formula is a finite rooted tree whose leaves are variables or constants in F and whose internal gates are binary addition or multiplication. Its output is a formal polynomial; equality means coefficientwise equality in \(F[x]\), also when F is finite. Its size is its number of nodes. An algebraic branching program is a finite directed acyclic graph with a designated source and sink and affine-linear polynomial labels on edges. It computes the sum, over all source-to-sink paths, of the product of the labels on that path. Count vertices, edges and the nonzero coefficients used to describe edge labels as its size; these choices differ only polynomially from the usual size conventions. Field constants have unit algebraic cost, with no bit-length bound. \(VF_{F}\) and \(VBP_{F}\) consist respectively of the polynomial families with formula size and branching-program size bounded by \(n^{b}+b\) for some constant b independent of n. These are nonuniform classes: a different finite computation may be chosen for each n, with no requirement to generate it algorithmically. The separation asks for one family in \(VBP_{F}\) for which, for every b, some n requires formula size greater than \(n^{b}+b\). There is no restriction to multilinear computation, bounded depth, homogeneous intermediate gates or noncommuting variables.
answer_criterion: For the stated field F, prove \(VF_{F} \subsetneq  VBP_{F}\) by exhibiting a family in \(VBP_{F}\) and proving that its formula sizes are not polynomially bounded, or prove \(VF_{F}=VBP_{F}\) by showing that every polynomial-size branching-program family has polynomial-size formulas. Any characteristic or field restriction must be stated as part of the scope of the answer. A lower bound only for bounded-depth or multilinear formulas does not resolve the unrestricted question.
